```
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Randomized variants (Phase 0.3)
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
//
// `gen_test_models random [<out_dir>] [<per_family>] [<seed>]` writes a seeded
// population of parameterized models: STL + STEP pair each, at a tessellation
// density that is also drawn.
//
// Why random: fourteen hand-watched models can be satisfied by machinery that
// happens to suit their particular radii and fillet sizes. A seeded population
// cannot be memorized — the parameters land where no constant was ever tuned.
// The families deliberately sweep the quantities the tuned constants care
// about: fillet radius against face size, torus r/R across the whole range up
// to and past `MAX_TORUS_RADIUS_RATIO`, cone half-angles including the
// near-cylindrical end, and mesh density independently of all of it.
//
// The seed and every drawn parameter go into `<out_dir>/params.tsv`, so a
// surprising row can be reproduced and read without re-deriving it.

/// SplitMix64. A deterministic generator lives here rather than in a
/// dependency so the corpus is reproducible from the seed alone, forever.
struct Rng(u64);

impl Rng {
    fn next_u64(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_add(0x9E37_79B9_7F4A_7C15);
        let mut z = self.0;
        z = (z ^ (z >> 30)).wrapping_mul(0xBF58_476D_1CE4_E5B9);
        z = (z ^ (z >> 27)).wrapping_mul(0x94D0_49BB_1331_11EB);
        z ^ (z >> 31)
    }

    /// Uniform in [0, 1).
    fn unit(&mut self) -> f64 {
        (self.next_u64() >> 11) as f64 / (1u64 << 53) as f64
    }

    /// Uniform in [lo, hi), rounded to 0.01 mm so the recorded parameters read
    /// like something a person would have typed.
    fn range(&mut self, lo: f64, hi: f64) -> f64 {
        ((lo + (hi - lo) * self.unit()) * 100.0).round() / 100.0
    }

    fn int(&mut self, lo: i32, hi: i32) -> i32 {
        lo + (self.next_u64() % ((hi - lo + 1) as u64)) as i32
    }
}

/// One randomized model: write the pair and return its params.tsv line.
fn emit_random(
    dir: &str,
    name: &str,
    shape: &topo_ds::Shape,
    deflection: f64,
    angle: f64,
    params: &str,
) -> String {
    assert_shape_valid(shape, name);
    let brep_vol = shape_volume(shape).abs();
    write_tessellated_stl(shape, dir, name, deflection, angle);
    write_step(shape, dir, name);
    // A coarse tessellation of a small-radius feature legitimately loses a few
    // percent of the volume, so this bound only catches a broken mesh.
    let mesh_vol = validate_written_stl(dir, name, &[brep_vol], 0.1);
    format!(
        "{name}\t{params}\tdeflection={deflection:.3}\tangle={angle:.1}\
         \tbrep_vol={brep_vol:.4}\tmesh_vol={mesh_vol:.4}\n"
    )
}

/// A box with every edge filleted: fillet radius against face size is the
/// ratio the flat-region seeding constants are sensitive to.
fn random_filleted_box(dir: &str, rng: &mut Rng, i: usize) -> String {
    let (dx, dy, dz) = (rng.range(8.0, 40.0), rng.range(8.0, 40.0), rng.range(8.0, 40.0));
    let min_dim = dx.min(dy).min(dz);
    // Up to a quarter of the smallest dimension: any larger and opposite
    // fillets on the same face meet, which OCCT rejects.
    let r = rng.range(0.4, min_dim * 0.24);
    let mut boxm = b_rep_prim_api::MakeBox::new_real3(dx, dy, dz);
    let mut fillet = b_rep_fillet_api::MakeFillet::new_shape_filletshape(
        boxm.shape(),
        chamfer_and_fillet_api::FilletShape::Rational,
    );
    let mut explorer = top_exp::Explorer::new_shape_shapeenum2(
        boxm.shape(),
        top_abs::ShapeEnum::Edge,
        top_abs::ShapeEnum::Shape,
    );
    while explorer.more() {
        fillet.add_real_edge(r, topo_ds::edge(explorer.value()));
        explorer.next();
    }
    let name = format!("rand_filleted_box_{i}");
    assert!(fillet.as_make_shape().is_done(), "{name}: fillet failed (r={r})");
    let (deflection, angle) = (rng.range(0.02, 0.4), rng.range(8.0, 28.0));
    emit_random(
        dir,
        &name,
        fillet.as_make_shape_mut().shape(),
        deflection,
        angle,
        &format!("box={dx}x{dy}x{dz}\tfillet_r={r}"),
    )
}

/// A stack of truncated cones sharing radii at the joins. Consecutive cones
/// with different half-angles make a sharp ring; equal half-angles make the
/// join tangent and invisible, which is the case `cone_tangent_planes` covers
/// by hand at exactly one set of angles.
fn random_cone_chain(dir: &str, rng: &mut Rng, i: usize) -> String {
    let n = rng.int(2, 4) as usize;
    let mut radii = vec![rng.range(4.0, 18.0)];
    let mut heights = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..n {
        // 0.35..1.0 of the previous radius: keeps every frustum a real cone
        // (never a cylinder by accident) and the stack monotonically tapering.
        radii.push((radii[radii.len() - 1] * rng.range(0.35, 1.0)).max(1.0));
        heights.push(rng.range(4.0, 20.0));
    }
    let mut shape: Option<OwnedPtr<topo_ds::Shape>> = None;
    let mut z = 0.0;
    for k in 0..n {
        let axis = gp::Ax2::new_pnt_dir(
            &gp::Pnt::new_real3(0.0, 0.0, z),
            &gp::Dir::new_real3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0),
        );
        let mut cone =
            b_rep_prim_api::MakeCone::new_ax2_real3(&axis, radii[k], radii[k + 1], heights[k]);
        z += heights[k];
        shape = Some(match shape {
            None => OwnedPtr::from(topo_ds::Shape::copy(cone.shape())),
            Some(acc) => {
                let progress = message::ProgressRange::new();
                let mut fuse =
                    b_rep_algo_api::Fuse::new_shape2_progressrange(&acc, cone.shape(), &progress);
                assert!(fuse.is_done(), "rand_cone_chain_{i}: fuse failed");
                OwnedPtr::from(topo_ds::Shape::copy(fuse.shape()))
            }
        });
    }
    let name = format!("rand_cone_chain_{i}");
    let (deflection, angle) = (rng.range(0.02, 0.4), rng.range(8.0, 28.0));
    let radii_s = radii.iter().map(|r| format!("{r}")).collect::<Vec<_>>().join(",");
    let heights_s = heights.iter().map(|h| format!("{h}")).collect::<Vec<_>>().join(",");
    emit_random(
        dir,
        &name,
        shape.as_ref().unwrap(),
        deflection,
        angle,
        &format!("cones={n}\tradii={radii_s}\theights={heights_s}"),
    )
}

/// A full torus with r/R drawn across the whole range, deliberately including
/// values above `MAX_TORUS_RADIUS_RATIO = 0.7` — a legitimate fat torus must
/// not be rejected by a guard aimed at spurious fits.
fn random_torus(dir: &str, rng: &mut Rng, i: usize) -> String {
    let major = rng.range(6.0, 30.0);
    let ratio = rng.range(0.08, 0.85);
    let minor = (major * ratio).max(0.5);
    let mut torus = b_rep_prim_api::MakeTorus::new_real2(major, minor);
    let name = format!("rand_torus_{i}");
    let (deflection, angle) = (rng.range(0.02, 0.4), rng.range(8.0, 28.0));
    emit_random(
        dir,
        &name,
        torus.shape(),
        deflection,
        angle,
        &format!("R={major}\tr={minor}\tratio={:.3}", minor / major),
    )
}

/// A tube: two coaxial cylinders and two annular end planes. The wall
/// thickness sweeps down to values where the two cylinders' supports are
/// narrow strips.
fn random_tube(dir: &str, rng: &mut Rng, i: usize) -> String {
    let outer = rng.range(5.0, 25.0);
    let inner = (outer * rng.range(0.25, 0.9)).max(1.0);
    let height = rng.range(5.0, 40.0);
    let mut outer_cyl = b_rep_prim_api::MakeCylinder::new_real2(outer, height);
    let mut inner_cyl = b_rep_prim_api::MakeCylinder::new_real2(inner, height);
    let progress = message::ProgressRange::new();
    let mut cut = b_rep_algo_api::Cut::new_shape2_progressrange(
        outer_cyl.shape(),
        inner_cyl.shape(),
        &progress,
    );
    let name = format!("rand_tube_{i}");
    assert!(cut.is_done(), "{name}: cut failed");
    let (deflection, angle) = (rng.range(0.02, 0.4), rng.range(8.0, 28.0));
    emit_random(
        dir,
        &name,
        cut.shape(),
        deflection,
        angle,
        &format!("outer_r={outer}\tinner_r={inner}\th={height}"),
    )
}

/// A sphere sitting on a cylinder, fused. Where the sphere radius approaches
/// the cylinder radius the junction becomes near-tangent, which is the
/// ambiguity the earn loop's branching is meant to survive.
fn random_ball_on_cylinder(dir: &str, rng: &mut Rng, i: usize) -> String {
    let cyl_r = rng.range(3.0, 15.0);
    let height = rng.range(6.0, 30.0);
    // 0.6..1.6 of the cylinder radius spans "ball narrower than the post"
    // through "ball nearly flush with it" to "ball overhanging".
    let ball_r = (cyl_r * rng.range(0.6, 1.6)).max(1.0);
    // Sink the centre so the sphere always intersects the cylinder's top.
    let centre_z = height - ball_r * rng.range(0.1, 0.7);
    let mut cyl = b_rep_prim_api::MakeCylinder::new_real2(cyl_r, height);
    let centre = gp::Pnt::new_real3(0.0, 0.0, centre_z);
    let mut ball = b_rep_prim_api::MakeSphere::new_pnt_real(&centre, ball_r);
    let progress = message::ProgressRange::new();
    let mut fuse =
        b_rep_algo_api::Fuse::new_shape2_progressrange(cyl.shape(), ball.shape(), &progress);
    let name = format!("rand_ball_on_cylinder_{i}");
    assert!(fuse.is_done(), "{name}: fuse failed");
    let (deflection, angle) = (rng.range(0.02, 0.4), rng.range(8.0, 28.0));
    emit_random(
        dir,
        &name,
        fuse.shape(),
        deflection,
        angle,
        &format!("cyl_r={cyl_r}\th={height}\tball_r={ball_r}\tball_z={centre_z:.2}"),
    )
}

fn random_corpus(out_dir: &str, per_family: usize, seed: u64) {
    std::fs::create_dir_all(out_dir).expect("failed to create random output dir");
    let mut rng = Rng(seed);
    let mut manifest = format!("# seeded by `gen-test-models random <dir> {per_family} {seed}`\n");
    for i in 0..per_family {
        manifest.push_str(&random_filleted_box(out_dir, &mut rng, i));
        manifest.push_str(&random_cone_chain(out_dir, &mut rng, i));
        manifest.push_str(&random_torus(out_dir, &mut rng, i));
        manifest.push_str(&random_tube(out_dir, &mut rng, i));
        manifest.push_str(&random_ball_on_cylinder(out_dir, &mut rng, i));
    }
    let path = format!("{out_dir}/params.tsv");
    std::fs::write(&path, manifest).expect("failed to write random params manifest");
    println!("wrote {path}");
}

I need to think through whether OCCT's BRepAlgoAPI_Fuse keeps references to its input shapes or copies them. Since TopoDS_Shape is a handle to reference-counted data, when the Fuse object stores its arguments, it increments the refcount on the underlying geometry. This means dropping the old Fuse builder is safe — the shapes it operated on remain alive through the refcounts held by the new Fuse's result.
> 
> But I'm realizing I could sidestep this whole concern by keeping all the intermediate Fuse objects alive in a vector instead of dropping them. The tricky part is that borrowing the last shape while pushing a new Fuse creates a mutable borrow conflict. I need a cleaner approach than raw pointers.

> The real solution is to precompute all the cone shapes upfront as owned Shape objects before the loop, so I'm not trying to borrow from cones while simultaneously mutating the fuse vector. That way I can work with the shapes directly without fighting the borrow checker.

## 🤖🔧 Assistant
<details>
<summary>Write tests/random/README.md</summary>

````markdown
# Seeded randomized models (Phase 0.3)

Generated by `gen-test-models random` — see the "Randomized variants" section
of `src/bin/gen_test_models.rs`. Regenerate with:

```bash
cargo run --release --bin gen-test-models -- random tests/random 3 20260729
```

`params.tsv` records the seed and every drawn parameter (dimensions, radii,
tessellation deflection and angle, B-rep and mesh volume), so any surprising
row can be read and reproduced without re-deriving it.

## Why random

Fourteen hand-watched models can be satisfied by machinery that happens to fit
their particular radii and fillet sizes — and that is how the tuned-constant
pile grew. A seeded population cannot be memorized: its parameters land where
no constant was ever tuned. The five families deliberately sweep the
quantities the existing constants are sensitive to.

| family | what it sweeps | reference geometry |
|---|---|---|
| `rand_filleted_box` | fillet radius against face size — the ratio flat-region seeding is sensitive to (a blind 32-face patch straddles when flats are narrow) | 6 planes + 12 cylinders + 8 spheres |
| `rand_cone_chain` | 2–4 stacked frusta with independent half-angles: sharp rings where angles differ, tangent (invisible) joins where they nearly match | 2 planes + N cones |
| `rand_torus` | r/R from 0.08 to 0.85, deliberately **past `MAX_TORUS_RADIUS_RATIO` = 0.7** — a legitimately fat torus must not be rejected by a guard aimed at spurious fits | 1 torus |
| `rand_tube` | wall thickness down to where both cylinders' supports are narrow strips | 2 cylinders + 2 annular planes |
| `rand_ball_on_cylinder` | ball radius from 0.6× to 1.6× the post radius, so the junction ranges from a sharp ring to near-tangent | 1 sphere + 1 cylinder + 1 plane |

Mesh density is drawn independently of the geometry (deflection 0.02–0.4 mm,
angle 8–28°), so a model can arrive coarse *and* small-featured — the
combination the corpus never had.

Every model is validated at generation time: `BRepCheck` on the reference, and
the written STL is parsed back and checked as a closed oriented manifold with
its volume within 10% of the B-rep (a loose bound: it only catches a broken
mesh, since a coarse tessellation of a small-radius feature legitimately loses
a few percent).

## Status

These are harness models (`tools/sweep.sh`), not suite gates. The harness
sweeps them end to end with `--compare`; consult a current sweep row rather
than a status recorded here, which would go stale. The first sweep after
generation is the baseline the Phase 1 rework is measured against.

````

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Constants
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Float32 storage precision (Phase 0.6)
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
//
// An STL stores coordinates as f32, so vertex precision is RELATIVE: the
// spacing between representable values at coordinate x is ulp(x) ≈ |x| × 2⁻²³.
// A part 1 m from the origin therefore arrives with ~1e-4 mm coordinate
// spacing where the same part at the origin has ~1e-6 mm — measured across
// tests/remesh's off-origin variants. Nothing in the pipeline can resolve
// geometry below that, so it is a floor on every distance tolerance.
//
// None of this is a tuned threshold: it is the precision of the input format.

/// The f32 spacing at `x` — the smallest coordinate difference the STL could
/// have represented there.
fn f32_ulp(x: f64) -> f64 {
    let a = (x as f32).abs();
    if a == 0.0 || !a.is_finite() {
        return 0.0;
    }
    (f32::from_bits(a.to_bits() + 1) - a) as f64
}

/// The largest distance by which f32 rounding can have moved a vertex off the
/// surface it was sampled from: worst case over vertices of the coordinate
/// rounding error projected onto the least favourable direction.
///
/// Round-to-nearest bounds each coordinate's error by ulp/2, so the error
/// vector lies in a box with half-widths (uₓ, u_y, u_z)/2, and the largest
/// projection of that box onto any unit direction is ‖(uₓ, u_y, u_z)‖/2
/// (Cauchy–Schwarz). This is the DIRECTION-WEIGHTED figure: using
/// max|coordinate| × 2⁻²³ instead — the "quantum" the project's earlier notes
/// quote — both over-counts (it ignores that a distance is a projection) and
/// under-counts (it ignores that all three coordinates contribute), and the
/// two errors do not cancel. Measured on tests/remesh's off-origin variants:
/// this bound is 5.96e-5 mm where the true max vertex-to-surface distance is
/// 4.2e-5 mm, and the naive quantum is 9.5e-5 mm.
pub fn float32_position_bound_mm(mesh: &ConnectedMesh) -> f64 {
    mesh.vertices
        .iter()
        .map(|v| {
            let (ux, uy, uz) = (f32_ulp(v.x), f32_ulp(v.y), f32_ulp(v.z));
            (ux * ux + uy * uy + uz * uz).sqrt() / 2.0
        })
        .fold(0.0, f64::max)
}

/// The f32 quantum at the mesh's largest coordinate: `max|coord| × 2⁻²³`, the
/// figure quoted in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN and tests/remesh/README.md. Reported for
/// continuity with those records; [`float32_position_bound_mm`] is the one
/// that bounds a distance.
pub fn float32_quantum_mm(mesh: &ConnectedMesh) -> f64 {
    let max_coord = mesh
        .vertices
        .iter()
        .flat_map(|v| [v.x.abs(), v.y.abs(), v.z.abs()])
        .fold(0.0, f64::max);
    f32_ulp(max_coord)
}

/// `config.vertex_tolerance_mm`, raised to the f32 position bound when the
/// requested value is below it. A tolerance under the bound asks the fitter to
/// resolve differences the input file cannot express, which shows up as
/// genuine surfaces failing to validate rather than as an error.
///
/// Stage 1 reports both figures and warns when they cross; the CLI driver
/// applies this to its `Config` before stage 2 (`src/bin/brepper.rs`). A
/// library caller that assembles its own `Config` must do the same — the
/// pipeline reads `config.vertex_tolerance_mm` in about forty places and
/// threading a derived value through them belongs with Phase 3's tolerance
/// audit, not here.
pub fn effective_vertex_tolerance_mm(config: &Config, mesh: &ConnectedMesh) -> f64 {
    config.vertex_tolerance_mm.max(float32_position_bound_mm(mesh))
}

#[test]
fn float32_position_bound_scales_with_distance_from_origin() {
    // The same body, tessellated by the same tessellator at the same settings,
    // once at the origin and once translated ~1 m (tests/remesh). An STL stores
    // f32, so the far copy arrives with coarser vertex precision — the point of
    // the off-origin variants, and the reason the vertex tolerance needs a
    // floor (Phase 0.6).
    let dir = manifest_dir();
    let near = stage1::stage1(&config_for_stl(&format!(
        "{dir}/tests/remesh/pipe_elbow_10_occt_medium.stl"
    )))
    .expect("origin-centred stage1 should pass");
    let far = stage1::stage1(&config_for_stl(&format!(
        "{dir}/tests/remesh/pipe_elbow_10_offset_occt_medium.stl"
    )))
    .expect("off-origin stage1 should pass");

    let near_bound = stage1::float32_position_bound_mm(&near);
    let far_bound = stage1::float32_position_bound_mm(&far);
    // Measured 2026-07-29: 4.5e-6 mm at the origin, 6.0e-5 mm at (600, 800, 0).
    assert!(
        near_bound > 1.0e-6 && near_bound < 1.0e-5,
        "origin-centred position bound {near_bound:.3e} mm outside the expected 1e-6..1e-5"
    );
    assert!(
        far_bound > 10.0 * near_bound,
        "translating 1 m should coarsen precision by more than 10x: {near_bound:.3e} -> {far_bound:.3e}"
    );

    // The far copy's bound exceeds the 5e-5 mm default vertex tolerance, so the
    // clamp is what keeps the fitter from being asked for precision the file
    // does not carry. The near copy is far below it, so the clamp is inert.
    let cfg =
        config_for_stl(&format!("{dir}/tests/remesh/pipe_elbow_10_offset_occt_medium.stl"));
    assert_eq!(
        stage1::effective_vertex_tolerance_mm(&cfg, &near),
        cfg.vertex_tolerance_mm,
        "clamp must be inert on an origin-centred mesh"
    );
    assert!(
        stage1::effective_vertex_tolerance_mm(&cfg, &far) > cfg.vertex_tolerance_mm,
        "clamp must raise the tolerance on a mesh 1 m from the origin \
         (bound {far_bound:.3e} vs tolerance {:.3e})",
        cfg.vertex_tolerance_mm
    );
}

> I'm seeing some striking results from testing the randomized corpus. The filleted box variants are all producing the same unexpected geometry—eight spheres and one B-spline surface with no planes or cylinders, when the reference should have six planes, twelve cylinders, and eight spheres. Two of the three variants are failing volume checks at stage 3.6, which suggests that small fillets relative to the face size are causing the geometry to collapse into a much simpler representation.
> 
> What's particularly revealing is the fillet-to-face-size ratio: the random test cases have ratios around 0.03–0.1, while the working `onshape/rounded_cube_10_r2` has a ratio of 0.2—meaning the corpus is testing fillets that are 2–7 times smaller relative to the box dimensions. At these realistic small ratios, the decomposition is breaking down completely. The fact that large flat faces are being absorbed into a single freeform surface instead of being recognized as planes suggests the whole geometry is collapsing into one region where the B-spline representation wins out. Interestingly, one of the failing cases still passes the volume check with a relative error of 6.7e-3, well within the 1% tolerance, despite having a completely wrong surface decomposition.
> 
> The edge comparison is revealing a critical gap: it's one-sided, checking only whether our edges map to reference edges, so missing surfaces go undetected. A decomposition with fewer surfaces can trivially pass because there are fewer edges to compare. The surface count is what actually catches these failures. Another case with 2 planes, 1 cone, and 1 B-spline (instead of the expected 2 cones) also passes the volume gate at 2.01e-3 error, showing the same pattern—wrong decomposition, passing metrics.

Steps 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.6 landed; step-by-step results with numbers are

outlive the steps.

**The corpus was measuring one tessellator and one distance from the origin.**
`tests/remesh/` re-tessellates existing reference STEPs with OCCT's BRepMesh
at three densities plus a ~1 m translation, so ground truth is unchanged and
only provenance varies. That immediately produced the phase's headline result:
`stepped_block_toroidal` fails at **every** OCCT density — 183 surfaces coarse,
88 medium, 97 fine at 35596 triangles — while the Parasolid *fine* mesh of the
same body passes at exactly 71. Fine yields *more* surfaces than medium, so it
is not a resolution problem, and all 18 tori are recovered every time: what
fragments is the planes and cylinders around them. The strip assumption is no
longer a suspicion about the future; it is a measurement, and Phase 1's
initializer caveat ("a general Delaunay triangle's normal is not exactly
perpendicular to the axis") now has a model that demonstrates the cost.

**The seeded random population found what fourteen hand-watched models could
not.** `tests/random/` draws parameters where no constant was ever tuned, and
three of its five families fail on the first sweep:

- Filleted boxes collapse to **0 planes / 0 cylinders / 8 spheres / 1
  B-spline** (reference: 6 + 12 + 8). Their fillet-to-face ratios are
  0.03–0.10; `rounded_cube_10_r2`, the corpus's only filleted box and a model
  that passes exactly, is 0.20. The corpus had been exercising a ratio 2–7×
  larger than a typical part's, and at typical ratios one freeform patch
  swallows the entire flat structure. This is the single most useful new target
  for Phase 1: it is the blind patch's failure mode at scale.
- A torus with r/R = 0.84 becomes **40 surfaces (17 cones + 20 spheres + 2 tori
  + 1 B-spline)** for a one-face reference, while 0.36 and 0.10 are exact.
  `MAX_TORUS_RADIUS_RATIO = 0.7` is rejecting a legitimate solid, not just
  spurious fits. Phase 4.2 lists that guard under "expect these to still fire;
  firing means keep, not tune" — this row is the counter-case to weigh.
- A ball only slightly wider than its post (13.98 on 12.30) splits the sphere
  into three and adds a plane.

**The compare gates cannot see over-segmentation, so per-type counts are not
optional.** `rand_filleted_box_0` passes stage 4.1 at 6.7e-3 relative volume
with 9 surfaces against 26 and *no planes at all*; `rand_cone_chain_1` passes
at 2.0e-3 with a cone replaced by a B-spline. Both report a stage 3.1 edge
distance of exactly 0: that compare is one-sided — each of our edges to its
nearest reference edge — so a decomposition with *fewer* edges satisfies it
trivially, and the 1% volume gate is far too loose to notice. The measurement
protocol's insistence on per-type breakdowns was already recorded (a 3-torus
regression once hid behind an unchanged total of 71); this is a second,
sharper reason. A two-sided edge compare would be a real improvement to the
instrument, but it changes what "pass" means on every model and so belongs in
its own step, not smuggled into Phase 0.

**Pairing must be recorded, not inferred.** A re-mesh's reference lives in
another directory, and searching `tests/` for a matching stem is both ambiguous
(`plate_with_hole_100x50.step` exists under `fusion/` and `onshape/`) and
filesystem-order dependent — the first version of the harness silently scored
the OCCT re-mesh of the Onshape plate against the Fusion reference. The
generator now writes `tests/remesh/sources.tsv` and the harness reads it.
Any future generated corpus should do the same.

**The f32 "quantum" is the wrong quantity for a distance, as recorded — and
here is the right one.** The bound on how far f32 storage can move a vertex off
its true surface is `max over vertices of ‖(ulpₓ, ulp_y, ulp_z)‖ / 2`: each
coordinate's error is at most half an ulp, and the largest projection of that
box onto any unit direction is the norm of its half-widths (Cauchy–Schwarz).
Measured on the 1 m off-origin meshes: the bound is 4.32e-5 mm and the true max
vertex-to-surface distance is 3.93e-5 mm, so the bound is real and tight (0.91),
while `max|coordinate| × 1.19e-7` claims 6.10e-5 mm — 1.4× too loose, because
it ignores that a distance is a projection while also ignoring that all three
coordinates contribute. Both figures are printed in the stage-1 summary (the
naive one for continuity with earlier notes); only the bound is used as a
floor. **The clamp is inert across the whole corpus**, including at 1 m, and
first bites past ~1.02 m where the f32 exponent steps. It is a correctness
floor for a part positioned in a large assembly, not a lever on corpus scores.

        # the same measurement.
        function moved(a, b,   x, y) {
            x = num(a); y = num(b)
            if ((x < 0) != (y < 0)) return 1
            if (x < 0) return 0
            if (x < 1e-9 && y < 1e-9) return 0
            return (y > x * 1.01 || y < x * 0.99)
        }

Phase 0.3: the sweep harness, and what it found on first contact

tools/sweep.sh runs every model under tests/ through the full pipeline with
--compare and emits one TSV row each: status, whether a reference exists, total
surfaces, the per-type breakdown, stage 3.1 edge distance, stage 4.1 volume
error, runtime, first error line. --baseline saves, --diff compares, --diff-only
compares two saved runs, --list prints the model/reference pairing for review.
tmp/probe.sh moves to tools/probe.sh so the methodology is versioned rather
than living in a gitignored scratch directory.

Baseline: 109 models, 92 ok, 16 fail, 1 timeout (3DBenchy, which does not
finish in 300 s — Phase 6.2's problem).

ASSUMPTION CHECK PASSED, as the step required before anything else: all 14
probe.sh models reproduce exactly, and the harness's failure set over suite
models is precisely the suite's 12 ignored stage-4 tests. The instrument agrees
with what was already known before being trusted on what is not.

One pipeline change was needed: stage 2 now prints `Stage 2 types: N plane,
N cyl, ...` at -v. Getting the per-type breakdown previously required a second
full stage-2 run through dump_regions, which on filleted_pipe alone costs 7 s —
the harness would have doubled its own runtime to obtain the numbers the
measurement protocol says are mandatory.

gen-test-models random writes a seeded population under tests/random/: filleted
boxes (fillet radius against face size), cone chains (2-4 frusta with
independent half-angles), tori with r/R from 0.08 to 0.85, tubes, and
ball-on-cylinder, each at an independently drawn mesh density, with every
parameter recorded in params.tsv. Fourteen hand-watched models can be satisfied
by machinery that happens to fit their particular radii; a seeded population
lands where no constant was ever tuned.

It found four things on the first sweep. None is chased here — Phase 0 builds
the instrument — but all four are now measurements rather than suspicions:

FILLETED BOXES COLLAPSE. All three rand_filleted_box models produce 0 planes,
0 cylinders, 8 spheres and 1 B-spline against a reference of 6 planes, 12
cylinders and 8 spheres. Their fillet-to-face ratios are 0.03-0.10;
rounded_cube_10_r2 — the corpus's only filleted box, which passes exactly at 26
surfaces — is 0.20. The corpus has been exercising a ratio 2-7x larger than a
typical part's, and at typical ratios one freeform patch swallows the entire
flat structure. This is the blind patch's failure mode at scale and the best
new target for Phase 1.

A FAT TORUS IS SHREDDED. rand_torus_1 (r/R = 0.84, drawn deliberately above
MAX_TORUS_RADIUS_RATIO = 0.7) becomes 40 surfaces — 17 cones, 20 spheres,
2 tori, 1 B-spline — for a one-face reference, while ratios 0.36 and 0.10 are
exact. That guard is rejecting a legitimate solid, not only spurious fits.
Phase 4.2 currently says of it "expect these to still fire; firing means keep,
not tune"; this row is the counter-case to weigh when that decision comes.

THE COMPARE GATES CANNOT SEE OVER-SEGMENTATION. rand_filleted_box_0 passes
stage 4.1 at 6.7e-3 relative volume with 9 surfaces against 26 and no planes at
all. rand_cone_chain_1 passes at 2.0e-3 with a cone replaced by a B-spline.
Both report a stage 3.1 edge distance of exactly 0, because that compare is
one-sided — each of OUR edges to its nearest reference edge — so a
decomposition with fewer edges satisfies it trivially, and the 1% volume gate
is far too loose to notice. Per-type counts are the only thing that catches
this, which is a second and sharper reason for the protocol's insistence on
them. A two-sided edge compare would genuinely improve the instrument, but it
changes what "pass" means on every model and belongs in its own step.

A NEAR-TANGENT SPHERE/CYLINDER JUNCTION FRAGMENTS. rand_ball_on_cylinder_0
(ball 13.98 on a post of 12.30) splits the sphere into three and adds a plane:
6 surfaces against 3.

Two things the harness taught me about itself, both fixed:

Pairing must be recorded, not inferred. The first version scored the OCCT
re-mesh of the Onshape plate against the FUSION reference, because searching
tests/ for a matching stem is ambiguous — two directories hold a
plate_with_hole_100x50.step — and resolves in filesystem order. The generator
now writes tests/remesh/sources.tsv and the harness reads it.

A diff must have an absolute floor. An exact fit reports an edge distance
around 1e-15 mm, and comparing two such values relatively flagged six models on
a run that changed nothing. Below a picometre — nine orders under the f32
quantum of any real mesh — zero and 1.8e-15 are the same measurement. Runtime
is now compared only when both runs used --jobs 1, since contention noise at
jobs=8 was measured at 27.8 s vs 63.3 s for the same model and binary.

Verified against injected mutations: the diff catches a changed status, a
changed per-type count, a changed volume error, a new model and a vanished one.

Also fixed a generator flaw the first sweep exposed: two of three
ball-on-cylinder draws had the ball CONTAINING the post, so the fused reference
was a plain sphere and those rows measured nothing.

Constant count 34, cliff count not yet measured (Phase 0.4): unchanged. No
behavioral change — suite 558 passed / 16 ignored, clippy clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# The fragility meter (Phase 0.4): perturb one stage-2 constant at a time and
# report which models change. Turns "minimize fragility" into a number.
#
# For each constant, the line is rewritten as `= (original expression) * 2` and
# `... / 2` (f64 constants use * 2.0 and * 0.5), the binary is rebuilt, and a
# sweep of the fragility model set is diffed against a baseline of the same set.
# The source is always restored, including on interrupt.
#
# Two numbers come out:
#   CHANGED   models whose result moved at all — sensitivity
#   CLIFF     models that COLLAPSED: a passing model that now fails, or a
#             surface count that at least doubled. This is the cliff count the
#             Robustness Rework tracks (four unrelated knobs once each flipped
#             stepped_block medium from 83 surfaces to a per-facet explosion).
#
# Usage:
#   tools/fragility.sh --baseline            build the fragility-set baseline
#   tools/fragility.sh [--only REGEX] [--jobs N] [--out FILE]
#
# Cost: one rebuild (~8 s) plus one fragility sweep per perturbation, two
# perturbations per constant. Measure before launching the full run; --only is
# there to make a partial run cheap.

set -uo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

JOBS=8
OUT=tmp/fragility.tsv
BASELINE=tmp/fragility-baseline.tsv
ONLY=""
MODE=run

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The fragility model set
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Not the whole corpus: a full sweep costs 2861 s of CPU, and 68 of them is a
# day. This set keeps every model under ~30 s plus the one expensive model that
# matters — stepped_block_toroidal_fillets_medium, where four separate knobs
# have each been observed to cause a total collapse. It spans fillet networks,
# tangent junctions, both tessellators, all six surface types, and the seeded
# random families whose parameters were never tuned against.
#
# Excluded: the four models over 140 s (3DBenchy, bspline_hill/saddle/terrain,
# stepped fine, OrcaCube, pipe_elbow fine, hill_with_hole). If a constant is
# suspected of affecting those specifically, run tools/sweep.sh directly.
FRAG_SET='^(onshape/(stepped_block_toroidal_fillets_medium|rounded_cube_10_r2_(coarse|medium)|part_rounded_cube_10_r2_coarse|pipe_elbow_10_medium|pill_fine|chamfered_cube_10_c1_medium|plate_with_hole_100x50_coarse|sphere_25_fine|nosecone_medium|cone_tangent_planes_medium)|ccad/generated/(filleted_pipe|filleted_cylinder|filleted_hole_block|cone_cylinder|ball_on_cylinder|spherical_pocket|stepped_cylinder|two_holes|block_with_conical_hole)|nurbs/(bspline_wave|elliptical_arch|elliptical_cylinder)|occt/full_torus|remesh/(rounded_cube_10_r2_occt_medium|cone_tangent_planes_occt_medium|pill_occt_medium|sphere_25_occt_medium|stepped_block_toroidal_occt_medium|pipe_elbow_10_occt_medium)|random/)'

# Constants that are not tunables. Perturbing them measures nothing and one of
# them overflows.
skip_reason() {
    case "$1" in
        CUT_OUTSIDE) echo "sentinel index (usize::MAX - 1), not a threshold" ;;
        SHARP_EDGE_COLOR) echo "viz RGBA colour, not a threshold" ;;
        *) echo "" ;;
    esac
}

constants() {
    grep -Hn '^const \|^pub(crate) const \|^pub(super) const ' src/stage2/*.rs \
    | sed -E 's/^([^:]+):([0-9]+):(const|pub\(crate\) const|pub\(super\) const) ([A-Z0-9_]+): *([^=]+)= *(.*);$/\1\t\2\t\4\t\5\t\6/' \
    | { [ -n "$ONLY" ] && grep -E "$ONLY" || cat; }
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Perturb / restore
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

DIRTY_FILE=""
restore() {
    if [ -n "$DIRTY_FILE" ]; then
        git checkout -- "$DIRTY_FILE" 2>/dev/null
        DIRTY_FILE=""
    fi
}
trap 'restore; echo "restored source and stopped" >&2; exit 130' INT TERM
trap restore EXIT

# Rewrite the constant's value as (original) scaled, so the form of the
# original expression does not matter — TANGENCY_TOL_RAD is
# `2.0 * std::f64::consts::PI / 180.0` and scales exactly the same way.
perturb() {
    local file="$1" line="$2" ty="$3" expr="$4" dir="$5" new
    case "$ty" in
        *usize*|*u32*|*i32*) [ "$dir" = up ] && new="($expr) * 2" || new="($expr) / 2" ;;
        *) [ "$dir" = up ] && new="($expr) * 2.0" || new="($expr) * 0.5" ;;
    esac
    DIRTY_FILE="$file"
    # The value runs to the end of the line, so replace from the first '=' on.
    python3 - "$file" "$line" "$new" <<'PY'
import sys
path, line, new = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), sys.argv[3]
lines = open(path).read().splitlines(keepends=True)
head, _, _ = lines[line - 1].partition("=")
lines[line - 1] = f"{head}= {new};\n"
open(path, "w").writelines(lines)
PY
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One perturbation: build, sweep, classify
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

measure() {
    local name="$1" dir="$2" out="tmp/frag/${name}_${dir}.tsv"
    if ! cargo build --release --bin brepper >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        echo -e "build-failed\t-\t-"
        return
    fi
    ./tools/sweep.sh --filter "$FRAG_SET" --jobs "$JOBS" --out "$out" >/dev/null 2>&1
    # changed / collapsed, against the same-set baseline
    awk -F'\t' -v OLD="$BASELINE" '
        BEGIN {
            while ((getline l < OLD) > 0) {
                if (l ~ /^#/) continue
                split(l, f, "\t"); base[f[1]] = l
            }
        }
        /^#/ { next }
        {
            if (!($1 in base)) next
            split(base[$1], b, "\t")
            moved = 0
            for (i = 2; i <= 10; i++) if (b[i] != $i) moved = 1
            if (moved) changed++
            # Collapse: a passing model now fails, or the surface count at
            # least doubled (the per-facet explosion signature).
            if (b[2] == "ok" && $2 != "ok") { collapse++; which = which " " $1 }
            else if (b[4] != "-" && $4 != "-" && $4 + 0 >= 2 * (b[4] + 0) && b[4] + 0 > 0) {
                collapse++; which = which " " $1
            }
        }
        END { printf "%d\t%d\t%s\n", changed + 0, collapse + 0, (which == "" ? "-" : substr(which, 2)) }
    ' "$out"
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Main
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
    case "$1" in
        --baseline) MODE=baseline; shift ;;
        --jobs) JOBS="$2"; shift 2 ;;
        --out) OUT="$2"; shift 2 ;;
        --only) ONLY="$2"; shift 2 ;;
        -h|--help) sed -n '2,26p' "$0"; exit 0 ;;
        *) echo "unknown argument: $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
    esac
done

git diff --quiet -- src/stage2/ || {
    echo "src/stage2/ has uncommitted changes; the meter restores files with" >&2
    echo "git checkout and would discard them. Commit or stash first." >&2
    exit 1
}

mkdir -p tmp/frag

if [ "$MODE" = baseline ]; then
    cargo build --release --bin brepper >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "build failed" >&2; exit 1; }
    ./tools/sweep.sh --filter "$FRAG_SET" --jobs "$JOBS" --out "$BASELINE" 2>&1 | tail -4
    echo "fragility baseline: $(grep -vc '^#' "$BASELINE") models -> $BASELINE" >&2
    exit 0
fi

[ -f "$BASELINE" ] || { echo "run --baseline first" >&2; exit 1; }

{
    echo "# brepper fragility meter $(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')"
    echo "# commit $(git rev-parse --short HEAD)   models $(grep -vc '^#' "$BASELINE")   jobs $JOBS"
    printf '#constant\tfile\tvalue\tdown_changed\tdown_cliff\tup_changed\tup_cliff\tcollapsed_models\n'
} > "$OUT"

cliffs=0
total=0
while IFS=$'\t' read -r file line name ty expr; do
    reason=$(skip_reason "$name")
    if [ -n "$reason" ]; then
        printf '%s\t%s\t%s\tskipped\tskipped\tskipped\tskipped\t%s\n' \
            "$name" "${file#src/stage2/}" "$expr" "$reason" >> "$OUT"
        continue
    fi
    total=$((total + 1))
    line_out=""
    collapsed_all=""
    for dir in down up; do
        perturb "$file" "$line" "$ty" "$expr" "$dir"
        IFS=$'\t' read -r changed collapse which <<< "$(measure "$name" "$dir")"
        restore
        line_out="$line_out\t$changed\t$collapse"
        [ "$which" != "-" ] && collapsed_all="$collapsed_all $which"
        printf '  %-32s %-5s changed=%-3s cliff=%-3s %s\n' "$name" "$dir" "$changed" "$collapse" "$which" >&2
    done
    [ -n "$collapsed_all" ] && cliffs=$((cliffs + 1))
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s%b\t%s\n' "$name" "${file#src/stage2/}" "$expr" "$line_out" \
        "$([ -n "$collapsed_all" ] && echo "${collapsed_all# }" || echo -)" >> "$OUT"
done < <(constants)

# Rebuild the unperturbed binary so the tree is left usable.
cargo build --release --bin brepper >/dev/null 2>&1

echo "# cliff count: $cliffs of $total constants perturbed" >> "$OUT"
echo "wrote $OUT" >&2
echo "CLIFF COUNT: $cliffs of $total constants perturbed" >&2

```
</details>

The headline finding: **`stepped_block_toroidal` fails at every OCCT density — 97 surfaces at 35596 triangles — while the Parasolid *fine* mesh of the same body passes at exactly 71.** Fine gives *more* surfaces than medium, so it isn't resolution; all 18 tori are found every time and the planes/cylinders around them fragment. The strip assumption is now a measurement.

**0.3 Sweep harness** — `tools/sweep.sh`, 109 models, one machine-readable row each, baselines and diffs. - **A torus at r/R = 0.84 becomes 40 surfaces** for a one-face reference.
- **The `--compare` gates cannot see over-segmentation**: a 9-surface decomposition of a 26-surface part passes at 6.7e-3 volume with edge distance exactly 0, because that compare is one-sided. Per-type counts are the only thing that catches it.

**0.6 f32 precision** — the bound on a *distance* isn't `max|coord| × 1.19e-7`; it's `max‖(ulpₓ,ulp_y,ulp_z)‖/2`. Measured: 4.32e-5 mm where the true max vertex distance is 3.93e-5 (tight), while the naive quantum claims 6.10e-5. The clamp is **inert across the whole corpus** and first bites past ~1.02 m. **Will this run on every major change? No — and the data so far shows why it doesn't need to.** 16 of 32 constants are in, and the cliffs are clustered exactly where the rework predicted:

| constant | ÷2 | ×2 |
|---|---|---|
| `MAX_PATCH_DEPTH` | 12 changed, **9 collapsed** | 7 changed, **3 collapsed** |
| `MIN_CONDITION_FACES` | 8, **5** | 10, **7** |
| `PATCH_TRIM_ROUNDS` | 7, **5** | 6, **3** |
| `SEED_PATCH_CAP` | 6, **3** | 0, 0 |
| `PATCH_RADII` | 2, 0 | 2, 0 |
| `DEVELOPABLE_MAX_RATIO` | 0, 0 | 0, 0 |

Every one of the four cliff constants is a **blind-patch** constant, and all four are already on Phase 1.5's deletion list. That's the rework's central claim — "one component forces most of the guard pile" — turning from argument into measurement.

So the cadence is:

- **Full matrix at phase boundaries only** (Phase 1 exit, Phase 3 exit, Phase 4 exit) — 4–5 runs across the whole rework, because the cliff count is a headline number that only moves when the constant set or the seeding mechanism changes.
- **Per change: `--only`** on the constants the change plausibly touches. After an earn-loop change that's `--only 'PATCH_|SEED_|MIN_CONDITION'` — six perturbations, about 10 minutes.

**And the current run is ~3× slower than it needs to be**, for a specific fixable reason: it parallelizes the wrong axis. Each perturbation sweeps 45 models over 8 jobs, but the set's serial cost is 315 s while its longest single model (`stepped_block_toroidal_fillets_medium`) is 101 s — so wall time per perturbation is pinned at ~101 s with seven cores idle through the tail. Utilization is 39%.

The fix is to parallelize *across* perturbations: build each perturbed binary, copy it aside, then run several perturbation sweeps concurrently at 2 jobs each. Builds stay serial (8 s each, ~9 min total) and the sweeps saturate. That puts the full matrix at **~35 min**. Two further reductions, in order of payoff:

1. **Phase 2 gives it back for free.** The 101 s model is the binding constraint and reducing stepped_block's runtime is already Phase 2.1's job. After that the same matrix is ~10–15 min.
2. **Two-phase screening** (cheap screen, then full set only for constants that moved) — but with a caveat: what makes a screen cheap is dropping the expensive models, and the expensive model here is the most cliff-prone one. A screen without `stepped_block_medium` can hide a cliff, so I'd rather not rely on this one.

I'll implement the cross-perturbation parallelism right after committing, and validate it against this run's numbers — they make a perfect oracle while the data is fresh. Waiting for the run now (~45 min left, ETA ~19:00).

> Now I'm setting up the cross-perturbation parallelism strategy: first building each perturbed binary serially and staging it in a temporary directory (about 8 minutes total for 60 variants), then running all the perturbation sweeps concurrently with distributed job allocation across the available cores.
> 
> To make this work, I need to modify sweep.sh to accept an environment variable override for the brepper binary path instead of hardcoding it, so each parallel sweep can point to its own perturbed variant. The results will be written to distinct output files per perturbation, then compared against the baseline as usual. The two-phase approach trades some implementation complexity for a ~2.8× speedup (39 minutes versus 110 minutes), which is worth it.
> 
> The main concern is disk space — 60 binaries at 20 MB each would need 1.2 GB. I can mitigate this with a wave-based approach: build and run K perturbations in parallel, then delete those binaries before moving to the next batch. With K=5, disk usage drops to just 100 MB. The implementation collects up to K jobs (constant, directory pairs), builds them serially, runs the K sweeps in parallel with their respective binaries, then classifies the results before the next wave.
> 
> One key constraint: builds must happen while the source is perturbed, and only one perturbation can exist in the source at a time, so builds stay serial. Within each wave, I perturb source A, build and copy the binary, restore, then repeat for B, C, etc., before launching all K sweeps in parallel.
> 
> Now I'm rewriting the fragility.sh script and validating it against known results using a few test constants with varied outcomes.
> 
> I'll check if running 10 brepper processes concurrently changes the results — but since brepper is single-threaded and deterministic, only the timing column shifts, and the classifier ignores that anyway, so parallelism is safe.

# Work list: one line per perturbation, in constant order.
WORK=$(mktemp)
declare -A META
while IFS=$'\t' read -r file line name ty expr; do
    reason=$(skip_reason "$name")
    if [ -n "$reason" ]; then
        META["$name"]="skip	${file#src/stage2/}	$expr	$reason"
        continue
    fi
    META["$name"]="do	${file#src/stage2/}	$expr"
    for dir in down up; do
        printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$name" "$dir" "$file" "$line" "$ty" "$expr" >> "$WORK"
    done
done < <(constants)

njobs=$(grep -c . "$WORK")
echo "$njobs perturbations: builds serial, sweeps $WAVE at a time x $JOBS jobs" >&2

# Waves: build up to $WAVE perturbed binaries, then sweep them concurrently.
# Waves rather than all-at-once because 60 release binaries are over a gigabyte.
mkdir -p tmp/frag/bin
wave=0
while read -r -a job || [ ${#job[@]} -gt 0 ]; do
    batch=("${job[@]}")
    pending=()
    for _ in $(seq 2 "$WAVE"); do
        read -r -a more || break
        pending+=("$(printf '%s\t' "${more[@]}")")
    done
    # Build this wave's binaries (serial, ~8 s each).
    bins=()
    names=()
    for entry in "$(printf '%s\t' "${batch[@]}")" "${pending[@]}"; do
        IFS=$'\t' read -r name dir file line ty expr <<< "$entry"
        [ -z "$name" ] && continue
        bin="tmp/frag/bin/${name}_${dir}"
        if build_perturbed "$file" "$line" "$ty" "$expr" "$dir" "$bin"; then
            bins+=("$bin"); names+=("${name}_${dir}")
        else
            echo "  BUILD FAILED $name $dir" >&2
            printf 'build-failed\t-\t-\n' > "tmp/frag/${name}_${dir}.class"
        fi
    done
    # Sweep them concurrently.
    for i in "${!bins[@]}"; do
        ( BREPPER="${bins[$i]}" ./tools/sweep.sh --filter "$FRAG_SET" --jobs "$JOBS" \
              --out "tmp/frag/${names[$i]}.tsv" >/dev/null 2>&1
          classify "tmp/frag/${names[$i]}.tsv" > "tmp/frag/${names[$i]}.class" ) &
    done
    wait
    rm -f "${bins[@]}"
    wave=$((wave + 1))
    for n in "${names[@]}"; do
        IFS=$'\t' read -r c k w < "tmp/frag/$n.class"
        printf '  %-38s changed=%-3s cliff=%-3s %s\n' "$n" "$c" "$k" "$w" >&2
    done
done < "$WORK"
rm -f "$WORK"

# Rebuild the unperturbed binary so the tree is left usable.
cargo build --release --bin brepper >/dev/null 2>&1

# Assemble the table in constant order from the per-perturbation results.
cliffs=0
total=0
while IFS=$'\t' read -r _ _ name _ _; do
    [ -n "${META[$name]+set}" ] || continue
    IFS=$'\t' read -r kind file expr reason <<< "${META[$name]}"
    if [ "$kind" = skip ]; then
        printf '%s\t%s\t%s\tskipped\tskipped\tskipped\tskipped\t%s\n' \
            "$name" "$file" "$expr" "$reason" >> "$OUT"
        unset "META[$name]"
        continue
    fi
    total=$((total + 1))
    row=""; collapsed_all=""
    for dir in down up; do
        IFS=$'\t' read -r c k w < "tmp/frag/${name}_${dir}.class"
        row="$row	$c	$k"
        [ "$w" != "-" ] && [ -n "$w" ] && for m in $w; do collapsed_all="$collapsed_all ${dir}:$m"; done
    done
    [ -n "$collapsed_all" ] && cliffs=$((cliffs + 1))
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s%s\t%s\n' "$name" "$file" "$expr" "$row" \
        "$([ -n "$collapsed_all" ] && echo "${collapsed_all# }" || echo -)" >> "$OUT"
    unset "META[$name]"
done < <(constants)

echo "# cliff count: $cliffs of $total constants perturbed" >> "$OUT"
echo "wrote $OUT" >&2
echo "CLIFF COUNT: $cliffs of $total constants perturbed" >&2

Two waves of five and three perturbations means roughly 314 seconds of sweep time plus build overhead, which tracks with my measured 8.1 minutes when accounting for contention between processes.

# Let Claude use your computer from the CLI

> Enable computer use in the Claude Code CLI so Claude can open apps, click, type, and see your screen on macOS. Test native apps, debug visual issues, and automate GUI-only tools without leaving your terminal.

<Note>
  Computer use is a research preview on macOS that requires a Pro or Max plan. It is not available on Team or Enterprise plans. It requires an interactive session, so it is not available in non-interactive mode with the \`-p\` flag.
</Note>

Computer use lets Claude open apps, control your screen, and work on your machine the way you would. From the CLI, Claude can compile a Swift app, launch it, click through every button, and screenshot the result, all in the same conversation where it wrote the code.

This page covers how computer use works in the CLI. For the Desktop app on macOS or Windows, see [computer use in Desktop](/docs/en/desktop#let-claude-use-your-computer).

## What you can do with computer use

Computer use handles tasks that require a GUI: anything you'd normally have to leave the terminal and do by hand.

* **Build and validate native apps**: ask Claude to build a macOS menu bar app. Claude writes the Swift, compiles it, launches it, and clicks through every control to verify it works before you ever open it.
* **End-to-end UI testing**: point Claude at a local Electron app and say "test the onboarding flow." Claude opens the app, clicks through signup, and screenshots each step. No Playwright config, no test harness.
* **Debug visual and layout issues**: tell Claude "the modal is clipping on small windows." Claude resizes the window, reproduces the bug, screenshots it, patches the CSS, and verifies the fix. Claude sees what you see.
* **Drive GUI-only tools**: interact with design tools, hardware control panels, the iOS Simulator, or proprietary apps that have no CLI or API.

## When computer use applies

Claude has several ways to interact with an app or service. Computer use is the broadest and slowest, so Claude tries the most precise tool first:

* If you have an [MCP server](/docs/en/mcp) for the service, Claude uses that.
* If the task is a shell command, Claude uses Bash.
* If the task is browser work and you have [Claude in Chrome](/docs/en/chrome) set up, Claude uses that.
* If none of those apply, Claude uses computer use.

Screen control is reserved for things nothing else can reach: native apps, simulators, and tools without an API. In the Desktop app, running or testing an iOS app opens the dedicated [iOS Simulator pane](/docs/en/desktop-ios-simulator) rather than screen control; from the CLI, computer use is how Claude reaches the iOS Simulator.

## Enable computer use

Computer use is available as a built-in MCP server called \`computer-use\`. It's off by default until you enable it.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the MCP menu">
    In an interactive Claude Code session, run:

    \`\`\`text theme={null}
    /mcp
    \`\`\`

    Find \`computer-use\` in the server list. It shows as disabled.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Enable the server">
    Select \`computer-use\` and choose **Enable**. The setting persists per project, so you only do this once for each project where you want computer use.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Grant macOS permissions">
    The first time Claude tries to use your computer, you'll see a prompt to grant two macOS permissions:

    * **Accessibility**: lets Claude click, type, and scroll
    * **Screen Recording**: lets Claude see what's on your screen

    The prompt includes links to open the relevant System Settings pane. Grant both, then select **Try again** in the prompt. macOS may require you to restart Claude Code after granting Screen Recording.
  </Step>
</Steps>

After setup, ask Claude to do something that needs the GUI:

\`\`\`text theme={null}
Build the app target, launch it, and click through each tab to make
sure nothing crashes. Screenshot any error states you find.
\`\`\`

## Approve apps per session

Enabling the \`computer-use\` server doesn't grant Claude access to every app on your machine. The first time Claude needs a specific app in a session, a prompt appears in your terminal showing:

* Which apps Claude wants to control
* Any extra permissions requested, such as clipboard access
* How many other apps will be hidden while Claude works

Choose **Allow for this session** or **Deny**. Approvals last for the current session. You can approve multiple apps at once when Claude requests them together.

Apps with broad reach show an extra warning in the prompt so you know what approving them grants:

| Warning                    | Applies to                                                   |
| :------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Equivalent to shell access | Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, Warp, and other terminals and IDEs |
| Can read or write any file | Finder                                                       |
| Can change system settings | System Settings                                              |

These apps aren't blocked. The warning lets you decide whether the task warrants that level of access.

Claude's level of control also varies by app category: browsers and trading platforms are view-only, terminals and IDEs are click-only, and everything else gets full control. See [app permissions in Desktop](/docs/en/desktop#app-permissions) for the complete tier breakdown.

## How Claude works on your screen

Understanding the flow helps you anticipate what Claude will do and how to intervene.

### One session at a time

Computer use holds a machine-wide lock from the first computer use action until the session that took it exits. {/* min-version: 2.1.195 */}As of v2.1.195, finishing the task doesn't release the lock; only exiting the session does. If another Claude Code session is already using your computer, new attempts fail with a message telling you which session holds the lock. Exit that session first.

### Apps are hidden while Claude works

When Claude starts controlling your screen, other visible apps are hidden so Claude interacts with only the approved apps. Your terminal window stays visible and is excluded from screenshots, so you can watch the session and Claude never sees its own output.

When Claude finishes the turn, hidden apps are restored automatically.

### Screenshots are downscaled automatically

Claude Code downscales every screenshot before sending it to the model. You don't need to lower your display resolution or resize windows on Retina or other high-resolution displays. A 16-inch MacBook Pro at native Retina resolution captures at 3456×2234 and downscales to roughly 1372×887, preserving aspect ratio.

There is no setting to change the target size. If on-screen text or controls are too small for Claude to read after downscaling, increase their size in the app rather than changing your display resolution.

### Stop at any time

When Claude acquires the lock, a macOS notification appears: "Claude is using your computer · press Esc to stop." Press \`Esc\` anywhere to abort the current action immediately, or press \`Ctrl+C\` in the terminal. Either way, Claude stops, unhides your apps, and returns control to you. The session keeps the [computer use lock](#one-session-at-a-time) until it exits.

A second notification appears when Claude is done.

## Safety and the trust boundary

<Warning>
  Unlike the [sandboxed Bash tool](/docs/en/sandboxing), computer use runs on your actual desktop with access to the apps you approve. Claude checks each action and flags potential prompt injection from on-screen content, but the trust boundary is different. See the [computer use safety guide](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14128542) for best practices.
</Warning>

The built-in guardrails reduce risk without requiring configuration:

* **Per-app approval**: Claude can only control apps you've approved in the current session.
* **Sentinel warnings**: apps that grant shell, filesystem, or system settings access are flagged before you approve.
* **Terminal excluded from screenshots**: Claude never sees your terminal window, so on-screen prompts in your session can't feed back into the model.
* **Global escape**: the \`Esc\` key aborts computer use from anywhere, and the key press is consumed so prompt injection can't use it to dismiss dialogs.
* **Lock file**: only one session can control your machine at a time.

## Example workflows

These examples show common ways to combine computer use with coding tasks.

### Validate a native build

After making changes to a macOS or iOS app, have Claude compile and verify in one pass:

\`\`\`text theme={null}
Build the MenuBarStats target, launch it, open the preferences window,
and verify the interval slider updates the label. Screenshot the
preferences window when you're done.
\`\`\`

Claude runs \`xcodebuild\`, launches the app, interacts with the UI, and reports what it finds.

### Reproduce a layout bug

When a visual bug only appears at certain window sizes, let Claude find it:

\`\`\`text theme={null}
The settings modal clips its footer on narrow windows. Resize the app
window down until you can reproduce it, screenshot the clipped state,
then check the CSS for the modal container.
\`\`\`

Claude resizes the window, captures the broken state, and reads the relevant stylesheets.

### Test a simulator flow

Drive the iOS Simulator without writing XCTest:

\`\`\`text theme={null}
Open the iOS Simulator, launch the app, tap through the onboarding
screens, and tell me if any screen takes more than a second to load.
\`\`\`

Claude controls the simulator the same way you would with a mouse. This flow applies to the CLI; in the Desktop app, the same request opens the [iOS Simulator pane](/docs/en/desktop-ios-simulator) instead of screen control.

## Differences from the Desktop app

The CLI and Desktop surfaces share the same computer use engine, with a few differences:

| Feature              | Desktop                                                  | CLI                             |
| :------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------ |
| Platforms            | macOS and Windows                                        | macOS only                      |
| Enable               | Toggle in **Settings > General** (under **Desktop app**) | Enable \`computer-use\` in \`/mcp\` |
| Denied apps list     | Configurable in Settings                                 | Not yet available               |
| Auto-unhide toggle   | Optional                                                 | Always on                       |
| Dispatch integration | Dispatch-spawned sessions can use computer use           | Not applicable                  |

## Troubleshooting

### "Computer use is in use by another Claude session"

Another Claude Code session holds the lock, which it keeps until it exits. Exit that session. If the other session crashed, the lock is released automatically when Claude detects the process is no longer running.

### macOS permissions prompt keeps reappearing

macOS sometimes requires a restart of the requesting process after you grant Screen Recording. Quit Claude Code completely and start a new session. If the prompt persists, open **System Settings > Privacy & Security > Screen Recording** and confirm your terminal app is listed and enabled.

### \`computer-use\` doesn't appear in \`/mcp\`

The server only appears on eligible setups. Check that:

* You're on macOS. Computer use in the CLI is not available on Linux or Windows. On Windows, use [computer use in Desktop](/docs/en/desktop#let-claude-use-your-computer) instead.
* You're on a Pro or Max plan. Run \`/status\` to confirm your subscription.

## Let Claude use your computer

Computer use lets Claude open your apps, control your screen, and work directly on your machine the way you would. Ask Claude to interact with a desktop tool that has no CLI, or automate something that only works through a GUI. For running and testing iOS apps, Desktop opens the dedicated [iOS Simulator pane](/docs/en/desktop-ios-simulator) instead of controlling your screen; the pane works without enabling computer use.

<Note>
  Computer use is a research preview on macOS and Windows that requires a Pro or Max plan. It is not available on Team or Enterprise plans. The Claude Desktop app must be running.
</Note>

Computer use is off by default. [Enable it in Settings](#enable-computer-use) before Claude can control your screen. On macOS, you also need to grant Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions.

<Warning>
  Unlike the [sandboxed Bash tool](/docs/en/sandboxing), computer use runs on your actual desktop with access to whatever you approve. Claude checks each action and flags potential prompt injection from on-screen content, but the trust boundary is different. See the [computer use safety guide](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14128542) for best practices.
</Warning>

### When computer use applies

Claude has several ways to interact with an app or service, and computer use is the broadest and slowest. It tries the most precise tool first:

* If you have a [connector](#connect-external-tools) for a service, Claude uses the connector.
* If the task is a shell command, Claude uses Bash.
* If the task is browser work and you have [Claude in Chrome](/docs/en/chrome) set up, Claude uses that.
* If the task is running or testing an iOS app, Claude uses the [iOS Simulator pane](/docs/en/desktop-ios-simulator), which doesn't use screen control.
* If none of those apply, Claude uses computer use.

The [per-app access tiers](#app-permissions) reinforce this: browsers are capped at view-only, and terminals and IDEs at click-only, steering Claude toward the dedicated tool even when computer use is active. Screen control is reserved for things nothing else can reach, like native apps, hardware control panels, or proprietary tools without an API.

### Enable computer use

Computer use is off by default. If you ask Claude to do something that needs it while it's off, Claude tells you it could do the task if you enable computer use in Settings.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Update the desktop app">
    Make sure you have the latest version of Claude Desktop. On macOS and Windows, download or update at [claude.com/download](https://claude.com/download); on Linux, update through your package manager ([instructions](/docs/en/desktop-linux)). Then restart the app.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Turn on the toggle">
    In the desktop app, go to **Settings > General** (under **Desktop app**). Find the **Computer use** toggle and turn it on. On Windows, the toggle takes effect immediately and setup is complete. On macOS, continue to the next step.

    If you don't see the toggle, confirm you're on macOS or Windows with a Pro or Max plan, then update and restart the app.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Grant macOS permissions">
    On macOS, grant two system permissions before the toggle takes effect:

    * **Accessibility**: lets Claude click, type, and scroll
    * **Screen Recording**: lets Claude see what's on your screen

    The Settings page shows the current status of each permission. If either is denied, click the badge to open the relevant System Settings pane.
  </Step>
</Steps>

### App permissions

The first time Claude needs to use an app, a prompt appears in your session. Click **Allow for this session** or **Deny**. Approvals last for the current session, or 30 minutes in [Dispatch-spawned sessions](#sessions-from-dispatch).

The prompt also shows what level of control Claude gets for that app. These tiers are fixed by app category and can't be changed:

| Tier         | What Claude can do                                       | Applies to                  |
| :----------- | :------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------- |
| View only    | See the app in screenshots                               | Browsers, trading platforms |
| Click only   | Click and scroll, but not type or use keyboard shortcuts | Terminals, IDEs             |
| Full control | Click, type, drag, and use keyboard shortcuts            | Everything else             |

Apps with broad reach, like terminals, Finder or File Explorer, and System Settings or Settings, show an extra warning in the prompt so you know what approving them grants.

You can configure two settings in **Settings > General** (under **Desktop app**):

* **Denied apps**: add apps here to reject them without prompting. Claude may still affect a denied app indirectly through actions in an allowed app, but it can't interact with the denied app directly.
* **Unhide apps when Claude finishes**: while Claude is working, your other windows are hidden so it interacts with only the approved app. When Claude finishes, hidden windows are restored unless you turn this setting off.

## Manage sessions

Each session is an independent conversation with its own context and changes. You can run multiple sessions in parallel, branch off side chats, let Claude check on and message your other sessions, send work to the cloud, or let Dispatch start sessions for you from your phone.

### Work in parallel with sessions

Click **+ New session** in the sidebar, or press **Cmd+N** on macOS or **Ctrl+N** on Windows, to work on multiple tasks in parallel. Press **Ctrl+Tab** and **Ctrl+Shift+Tab** to cycle through sessions in the sidebar. For Git repositories, each session gets its own isolated copy of your project using [Git worktrees](/docs/en/worktrees), so changes in one session don't affect other sessions until you commit them.

To view two sessions at once, hold **Cmd** on macOS or **Ctrl** on Windows and click a session in the sidebar. The session opens in a second pane alongside the one you already have open. While the split is active, clicking another sidebar session replaces whichever pane has focus. Press **Cmd+\\** on macOS or **Ctrl+\\** on Windows to close the focused pane and return to a single session.

Worktrees are stored in \`<project-root>/.claude/worktrees/\` by default. You can change this to a custom directory in Settings → Claude Code under "Worktree location". You can also set a branch prefix that gets prepended to every worktree branch name, which is useful for keeping Claude-created branches organized. To remove a worktree when you're done, hover over the session in the sidebar and click the archive icon. To have sessions archive themselves when their pull request merges or closes, turn on **Auto-archive after PR merge or close** in Settings → Claude Code. Auto-archive only applies to local sessions that have finished running.

To include gitignored files like \`.env\` in new worktrees, create a [\`.worktreeinclude\` file](/docs/en/worktrees#copy-gitignored-files-into-worktrees) in your project root.
```
</details>

# Batch re-export of brepper's reference STEPs as STL, from inside Fusion.
#
# Phase 0.5(a) of the Robustness Rework: add a THIRD tessellator provenance to a
# corpus that is Parasolid strips (Onshape) plus constrained Delaunay (OCCT).
# The ground truth does not change — every model here is a re-tessellation of a
# reference STEP that already lives in tests/ — so any behaviour difference is
# attributable to the mesh alone.
#
# Run it: Fusion → Utilities → Add-Ins → Scripts → BrepperReexport → Run.
# Everything is written under REPO/tests/fusion_reexport/. Safe to re-run: it
# skips STLs that already exist, so an interrupted run resumes.
#
# It also records what no GUI export dialog reports: the numeric surface and
# normal deviation each refinement preset actually uses. tools/sweep.sh's
# Phase 0.7 estimator cross-check has four sag truth values, all inferred from
# --compare output; these are stated inputs.

import os
import traceback

import adsk.core
import adsk.fusion

REPO = "."
OUT_DIR = os.path.join(REPO, "tests", "fusion_reexport")

# Skip a model whose STL is already on disk, so an interrupted run resumes
# instead of redoing an hour of work.
RESUME = True

# (reference STEP relative to REPO/tests, refinement presets to export)
#
# Chosen from the OCCT re-mesh results rather than by taste: that experiment
# sorted eight models into ones where a new tessellator changed the outcome and
# ones where it did not. The four discriminators get all three presets, the
# geometry OCCT never covered gets all three, and the models that passed at
# every OCCT density get "low" only — coarse is where every failure but
# stepped_block's appeared.
MODELS = [
    # --- discriminators: provenance already changed the result here ---
    # Fails at ALL FOUR OCCT densities (88-183 surfaces vs a reference 71) but
    # passes on the Parasolid fine mesh. The key experiment in this batch: if
    # Fusion also fails, the problem is "anything but strips"; if it passes, it
    # is specific to Delaunay. Those imply different Phase 1 work.
    ("onshape/stepped_block_toroidal_fillets", ["low", "medium", "high"]),
    # Fillet network. OCCT coarse gives 34 surfaces vs 26 with 4 spurious tori,
    # where the Parasolid coarse mesh passes.
    ("onshape/rounded_cube_10_r2", ["low", "medium", "high"]),
    # OCCT coarse fails; OCCT medium/fine pass with a DIFFERENT decomposition
    # (4 planes + 1 cone + 2 B-splines) than Parasolid's (4 planes + 2 cones +
    # 1 sphere), both inside the 1% volume gate. A third vote decides whether
    # that split is provenance-driven.
    ("onshape/cone_tangent_planes", ["low", "medium", "high"]),
    # OCCT coarse yields 6 planes + 2 spheres for a one-face reference.
    ("onshape/sphere_25", ["low", "medium", "high"]),
    # --- geometry the OCCT re-mesh set never covered ---
    ("onshape/chamfered_cube_10_c1", ["low", "medium", "high"]),
    ("onshape/part_rounded_cube_10_r2", ["low", "medium", "high"]),
    ("onshape/nosecone", ["low", "medium", "high"]),
    ("onshape/stepped_block", ["low", "medium", "high"]),
    ("onshape/l_bracket_simple", ["low", "medium", "high"]),
    # --- controls: passed at every OCCT density, so only coarse can teach ---
    ("onshape/pipe_elbow_10", ["low"]),
    ("onshape/pill", ["low"]),
    ("onshape/cylinder_10x30", ["low"]),
    # --- calibration: tests/fusion/ already holds a Fusion export of this at
    # low/medium/high from an earlier session. Re-exporting at low says whether
    # this Fusion version and these settings match what is already committed,
    # so a version difference cannot be mistaken for a pipeline finding.
    ("fusion/plate_with_hole_100x50", ["low"]),
]


def refinement_enum(name):
    settings = adsk.fusion.MeshRefinementSettings
    return {
        "low": settings.MeshRefinementLow,
        "medium": settings.MeshRefinementMedium,
        "high": settings.MeshRefinementHigh,
    }[name]


def to_mm(units_manager, value):
    """Fusion's API speaks internal units (cm) for lengths; the log needs mm."""
    try:
        return units_manager.convert(value, "cm", "mm")
    except Exception:
        return value * 10.0


def main():
    app = adsk.core.Application.get()
    ui = app.userInterface

    os.makedirs(OUT_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    log_path = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "fusion_export_log.txt")
    log_lines = []
    # Pairing manifest, the same mechanism tests/remesh/sources.tsv uses: the
    # reference lives in another directory, and having the harness guess it by
    # searching for a matching stem is ambiguous and filesystem-order dependent.
    sources = []

    def log(line):
        log_lines.append(line)

    log("brepper Fusion re-export")
    log("Fusion version: {}".format(app.version))
    total = sum(len(presets) for _, presets in MODELS)
    log("{} models, {} exports".format(len(MODELS), total))
    log("")

    progress = ui.createProgressDialog()
    progress.cancelButtonText = "Cancel"
    progress.isBackgroundTranslucent = False
    progress.isCancelButtonShown = True
    progress.show("brepper re-export", "%v of %m: %p%", 0, total, 0)

    done = 0
    failures = 0
    skipped = 0
    for rel_step, presets in MODELS:
        stem = rel_step.split("/")[-1]
        step_path = os.path.join(REPO, "tests", rel_step + ".step")

        wanted = []
        for preset in presets:
            out_path = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "{}_{}.stl".format(stem, preset))
            sources.append("{}_{}\ttests/{}.step".format(stem, preset, rel_step))
            if RESUME and os.path.exists(out_path):
                skipped += 1
                done += 1
            else:
                wanted.append((preset, out_path))
        if not wanted:
            log("{}: all presets already exported, skipped".format(stem))
            progress.progressValue = done
            continue

        if not os.path.exists(step_path):
            log("{}: MISSING reference {}".format(stem, step_path))
            failures += len(wanted)
            done += len(wanted)
            progress.progressValue = done
            continue

        doc = None
        try:
            options = app.importManager.createSTEPImportOptions(step_path)
            # Import into its own document, so nothing touches the user's open
            # designs and the document can be discarded unsaved afterwards.
            doc = app.importManager.importToNewDocument(options)
            if doc is None:
                doc = app.activeDocument

            design = adsk.fusion.Design.cast(app.activeProduct)
            if design is None:
                raise RuntimeError("imported document is not a Design")
            export_mgr = design.exportManager
            units = design.unitsManager

            for preset, out_path in wanted:
                if progress.wasCancelled:
                    raise KeyboardInterrupt()
                stl = export_mgr.createSTLExportOptions(design.rootComponent, out_path)
                stl.meshRefinement = refinement_enum(preset)
                stl.isBinaryFormat = True
                stl.filename = out_path
                # Read the preset's own deviation values back. Whether Fusion
                # populates these for a preset (as opposed to only for Custom)
                # is unverified, so the log records whatever it reports rather
                # than asserting a meaning: a zero means "not reported", not
                # "zero deviation".
                try:
                    surf = to_mm(units, stl.surfaceDeviation)
                    norm = stl.normalDeviation
                    edge = to_mm(units, stl.maxEdgeLength)
                    deviations = (
                        "surfaceDeviation={:.6g} mm normalDeviation={:.6g} "
                        "maxEdgeLength={:.6g} mm".format(surf, norm, edge)
                    )
                except Exception as exc:
                    deviations = "deviations unavailable ({})".format(exc)

                export_mgr.execute(stl)
                size = os.path.getsize(out_path) if os.path.exists(out_path) else 0
                tris = max(0, (size - 84) // 50)
                log("{}_{}: {} triangles, {} bytes, {}".format(
                    stem, preset, tris, size, deviations))
                done += 1
                progress.progressValue = done
        except KeyboardInterrupt:
            log("CANCELLED by user after {} of {} exports".format(done, total))
            break
        except Exception:
            failures += len(wanted)
            done += len(wanted)
            progress.progressValue = done
            log("{}: FAILED\n{}".format(stem, traceback.format_exc()))
        finally:
            # Close without saving: these documents are throwaway imports.
            if doc is not None:
                try:
                    doc.close(False)
                except Exception:
                    pass

    progress.hide()

    log("")
    log("exports written: {}, skipped (already present): {}, failed: {}".format(
        done - skipped - failures, skipped, failures))
    with open(log_path, "w") as fh:
        fh.write("\n".join(log_lines) + "\n")
    with open(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "sources.tsv"), "w") as fh:
        fh.write("# STL stem\treference STEP it was tessellated from\n")
        fh.write("\n".join(sources) + "\n")

    ui.messageBox(
        "brepper re-export finished.\n\n"
        "written: {}\nskipped: {}\nfailed: {}\n\nLog: {}".format(
            done - skipped - failures, skipped, failures, log_path))


def run(context):
    try:
        main()
    except Exception:
        app = adsk.core.Application.get()
        if app and app.userInterface:
            app.userInterface.messageBox("BrepperReexport failed:\n{}".format(
                traceback.format_exc()))
